b:
Childhood & Early Life

Thomas Wyatt was born around 1503 at Allington Castle in Kent, the son of Henry Wyatt, a man who had backed the wrong side in the Wars of the Roses, been tortured in the Tower by Richard III, and come out loyal to the Tudors with a pension and a seat on the council. His mother was Anne Skinner. Thomas grew up inside that world of favour, and learned young how fast it could be taken away.

He went to St John's College, Cambridge, as a teenager, learned Latin, French and Italian, and was at court before he was twenty. He was tall, handsome, good at music and sport, and could out-talk almost anyone. People noticed.

What He Did & Why He's Remembered

Wyatt brought the sonnet into English. On diplomatic trips to Italy he read Petrarch, and he came home translating and reworking him, bending English into shapes it hadn't held before. His lines can sound rough to modern ears, and that's part of the charm: he sounds like a man actually thinking while he's hurt, not a man performing it.

His poems circulated at court in manuscript and were not printed under his name until Tottel's Miscellany in 1557, fifteen years after he died. Everything we have of him we have because somebody copied it out.

Family Life

Around 1520 he was married to Elizabeth Brooke, daughter of Lord Cobham, a match arranged by the families. It went badly. By the middle of the 1530s he had left her, and she was publicly accused of adultery, though he later took her back on the king's order, and it seems on strict terms. They had a son, also Thomas, who would lead a rebellion against Queen Mary in 1554 and be executed for it.

Romantic Life

The poem everyone argues about is Whoso List to Hunt. It is almost certainly a translation of a Petrarch sonnet, but Wyatt changes the ending. The deer wears a collar reading Noli me tangere, for Caesar's I am. Readers have heard Anne Boleyn in it ever since: a woman he wanted, who belonged to the king. He may have loved her, or just wanted her, or just watched her. There is later gossip that they were lovers, but no hard proof.

What we do know is that in 1536, when Anne fell, Wyatt was arrested and held in the Tower. From his cell he could see the executions of the men accused with her. He wrote a line in Latin about it, that the innocent are surrounded by enemies. He was released, probably because Cromwell protected him, and he never wrote about it plainly again.

Life Until Death

After the Tower he went back to court and was sent as ambassador to Charles V in Spain, a miserable job with a boss who wrote him nagging letters. When Cromwell fell in 1540, Wyatt was arrested again, in 1541, accused of treason and of speaking ill of the king. He defended himself in a long and brilliant speech, and was acquitted. He was freed on condition that he take his wife back.

In the autumn of 1542 he was told to ride out to meet a Spanish envoy at Falmouth, and he rode hard in the heat, caught a fever, and died at Sherborne in Dorset in October. He was about thirty-nine. His friend the Earl of Surrey wrote a famous elegy for him.

Their Works

These are his words. They're written in the spelling of the surviving manuscripts and early editions, so you may have to read some lines twice.

The Long Love that in my thought doth Harbor
The longë love that in my thought doth harbour

And in mine hert doth keep his residence,

Into my face presseth with bold pretence

And therein campeth, spreading his banner.

She that me learneth to love and suffer

And will that my trust and lustës negligence

Be rayned by reason, shame, and reverence,

With his hardiness taketh displeasure.

Wherewithall unto the hert’s forest he fleeth,

Leaving his enterprise with pain and cry,

And there him hideth and not appeareth.

What may I do when my master feareth

But in the field with him to live and die?

For good is the life ending faithfully.
Whoso List to Hunt
Whoso list to hunt? I know where is an
hind!
But as for me, alas!  I may no more,
The vain travail hath wearied me so sore;
I am of them that furthest come behind.
Yet may I by no means my wearied mind
Draw from the deer, but as she fleeth afore
Fainting I follow; I leave off therefore,
Since in a net I seek to hold the wind.
Who list her hunt, I put him out of doubt
As well as I, may spend his time in vain!
And graven with diamonds in letters plain,
There is written her fair neck round about;
‘ Noli me tangere; for Cæsar’s I am,
And wild for to hold, though I seem tame.’
I Find no Peace
I find no peace, and all my war is done;
I fear and hope, I burn, and freeze like
ice;
I fly aloft, yet can I not arise;
And nought I have, and all the world I seize on,
That locks nor loseth, holdeth me in prison,
And holds me not, yet can I scape no wise:
Nor lets me live, nor die, at my devise,
And yet of death it giveth me occasion.
Without eye I see; without tongue I plain:
I wish to perish, yet I ask for health;
I love another, and thus I hate myself;
I feed me in sorrow, and laugh in all my pain.
Lo, thus displeaseth me both death and life,
And my delight is causer of this strife.
My Galley
My galley chargèd with forgetfulness
Thorough sharp seas, in winter nights doth pass
‘Tween rock and rock; and eke mine enemy, alas,
That is my lord, steereth with cruelness,
And every oar a thought in readiness,
As though that death were light in such a case.
An endless wind doth tear the sail apace
Of forcèd sighs and trusty fearfulness.
A rain of tears, a cloud of dark disdain,
Hath done the wearied cords great hinderance;
Wreathèd with error and eke with ignorance.
The stars be hid that led me to this pain.
Drownèd is reason that should me consort,
And I remain despairing of the port.
They Flee from Me
They flee from me, that sometime did me
seek,
With naked foot stalking within my
chamber:
Once have I seen them gentle, tame, and meek,
That now are wild, and do not once remember,
That sometime they have put themselves in danger
To take bread at my hand; and now they range
Busily seeking in continual change.
Thanked be Fortune, it hath been otherwise
Twenty times better; but once especial,
In thin array, after a pleasant guise,
When her loose gown did from her shoulders fall,
And she me caught in her arms long and small,
And therewithal sweetly did me kiss,
And softly said, ‘ Dear heart, how like you this?’
It was no dream; for I lay broad awaking:
But all is turn’d now through my gentleness,
Into a bitter fashion of forsaking;
And I have leave to go of her goodness;
And she also to use new fangleness.
But since that I unkindly so am served:
How like you this, what hath she now deserved?
Farewell, Love
Farewell, Love, and all thy laws for
ever;
Thy baited hooks shall tangle me no more.
Senec, and Plato, call me from thy lore,
To perfect wealth, my wit for to endeavour;
In blind error when I did persevere,
Thy sharp repulse, that pricketh aye so sore,
Taught me in trifles that I set no store;
But scaped forth thence, since, liberty is lever
Therefore, farewell! go trouble younger hearts,
And in me claim no more authority:
With idle youth go use thy property,2
And thereon spend thy many brittle darts:
For, hitherto though I have lost my time,
Me list no longer rotten boughs to clime.

Notice that I Find no Peace is nearly all Petrarch, and the translation is faithful, but Wyatt makes the contradictions feel like his. And in They Flee from Me, the last line turns it into a question that is half a threat. The woman who loosened her gown and whispered how like you this gets the question thrown back at her at the end. It is one of the most honest poems about being left in English.
